card.hook: You're strolling through Cardiff city centre, and there's a whole castle waiting at the end of the street. Rude not to take a photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement on Castle Street and face north towards the castle entrance gate. The street leads your eye straight up to the gatehouse.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the street, the gate and a bit of sky in one shot. If people or traffic squeeze your space, drop to 0.5x and keep the castle in the middle so the edges don't stretch, or try 2x for a tighter shot of the gatehouse.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the street up so it leads to the gate, then tap the gatehouse and slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out the stone.
card.best_time: Check the light on the day, and go a touch darker if the sky looks bright. Pavements get busy, so wait for a gap in the crowd or take a few shots and pick the one with the clearest view of the gate.
card.selfie_here: Head to the grass near the castle in Bute Park, where the castle rises directly behind you (the park starts at the back of the castle grounds). Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and try 0.5x to squeeze in more towers over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Pose on the Animal Wall just outside the castle entrance and ask a passer-by to frame the whole castle behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Cardiff Castle asks visitors not to use selfie sticks inside the castle buildings, and flash is discouraged there. Personal, non-commercial photography is welcome in the buildings and grounds. The Castle Street pavement is public, but the castle interior is ticketed, so check the official site for grounds access and closures.
card.challenge: Take three shots and see if you can catch the gate with not a single stranger walking through it.
card.good_to_know: The Normans built the first castle in the late 11th century, on top of a 3rd-century Roman fort. Later, the 3rd Marquess of Bute paid William Burges to remodel it in Gothic revival style, which is why you get medieval and Victorian in one view. During the Second World War, air raid shelters big enough for up to 1,800 people were built inside the walls, and the castle was given to the City of Cardiff in 1947.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement on Castle Street and face north towards the castle entrance gate. The street leads your eye straight up to the gatehouse.

card.hook: You'll back up as far as the pavement allows, and the Principality Stadium will still laugh at you for trying to fit it all in. Good news: a big curvy wall of steel makes a great photo anyway.
card.stand_here: Head to the spot near Millennium Walk, about 30 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map. Face north-east so the middle of the stadium fills the view, and angle the phone up a little to catch the roof line.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for one big shot, since you're close and it fits the most wall and roof. Then switch to 1x for details like gates and signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the stadium's vertical edges up with them so the walls don't lean in.
card.best_time: Soft light or a bit of cloud suits it nicely. On match or event days it's much busier and some areas may be closed off, so allow extra time and check the official site first.
card.selfie_here: Try the Wood Street bridge by the stadium gates, which is a likely spot for a selfie with the stadium in view. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the stadium over your shoulder. The Riverwalk beside the River Taff is also worth a go near sunset.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are on the banned list at stadium entry for concerts, though personal phone photos are allowed. Check the official site before you go on event days.
card.challenge: Catch a few people walking past a gate so the stadium towers over them, and see who can make the tiniest human look the most heroic.
card.good_to_know: The stadium opened in June 1999, built for that year's Rugby World Cup, on the Cardiff Arms Park site. It was called the Millennium Stadium until early 2016. It holds 73,931 people, making it the largest stadium in Wales, and it has a fully retractable roof.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the spot near Millennium Walk, about 30 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map. Face north-east so the middle of the stadium fills the view, and angle the phone up a little to catch the roof line.

card.hook: Look at the wall and you'll swear someone has sliced a sea cliff and stood it up in Cardiff Bay. That's the Wales Millennium Centre, and the slate comes in purple, blue, green, grey and black.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, which sits at the Wales Millennium Centre itself. Face north-east and the slate walls and the bronze-coloured dome will be in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole frontage, and switch to zoom 0.5x if you're too close to fit it all in. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the slate layers, the narrow windows and the dome.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the slate, then drag the brightness slider a touch darker so the bronze dome and the sky don't wash out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late afternoon light brings out the slate colours and the glow of the dome. Dusk is worth a go too (use night mode and lean on a wall to keep steady), but the slate looks dull on grey days, so check the weather first.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the fountain on the open forecourt in front of the building with the centre behind you, and let the sweeping slate and bronze curves fill the background. For a second option, take one on the Plass footbridge with the centre behind you, using the front camera (or 0.5x if your phone has it) to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand out on Roald Dahl Plass, the open plaza in front, so the whole building fits in the frame, while you stand in front of the centre.
card.rules_and_safety: Visitors say the Plass is safe from traffic, so it's a good spot for kids to run about. Check the official site before you go if you want to photograph inside.
card.challenge: Can you get all five slate colours (purple, blue, green, grey and black) into one close-up?
card.good_to_know: Wales Millennium Centre is Wales's national arts centre, and the first phase opened in November 2004. About 1,350 tonnes of Welsh slate went into the building. The Donald Gordon Theatre has 1,896 seats, and the whole site covers about 3 hectares.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, which sits at the Wales Millennium Centre itself. Face north-east and the slate walls and the bronze-coloured dome will be in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a low, modern building of glass and timber sitting right beside a red-brick Victorian-looking neighbour, with calm bay water behind them. That old-and-new pairing is the Senedd and the Pierhead Building, and it photographs nicely.
card.stand_here: Stand in Roald Dahl Plass, the open plaza on the waterfront in front of the Senedd, next to the Pierhead Building. Face the glass-and-timber frontage with the Pierhead Building alongside it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole frontage with the Pierhead Building beside it. If the plaza is busy, drop to 0.5x to keep both buildings and some sky in the frame. For details like the timber and glass, try 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the roof edge up with one of the lines so the building doesn't look tilted.
card.best_time: Sunrise and dusk are suggested for the bay views, and evening shots of the Senedd and Pierhead are common. There's no single best time, so try one early or late visit if you can.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Senedd steps on Pierhead Street, the iconic ones at the front of the building. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the Senedd in the picture behind you. The Queen had her picture taken on these steps when she opened the building in 2006.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Roald Dahl Plass to frame you with the Senedd in view, and suggest they pick an angle that fits the whole building.
card.rules_and_safety: The plaza is free and open to the public, but access inside the Senedd may be limited, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three frames as people cross the plaza and see which one makes the building look busiest and which makes it look calmest.
card.good_to_know: The Senedd is the home of the Welsh Parliament, which makes laws for Wales on devolved matters such as health, education and transport. It was created in 1999 and was called the National Assembly for Wales until May 2020, when it became Senedd Cymru. You'll see Welsh and English on the signs, as both are official languages of its business.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Roald Dahl Plass, the open plaza on the waterfront in front of the Senedd, next to the Pierhead Building. Face the glass-and-timber frontage with the Pierhead Building alongside it.

card.hook: Here's a nice trick: the lawn does half the work. Wide steps, tall columns and a strip of grass in front give you a calm, symmetrical shot that looks like you planned it.
card.stand_here: Stand in Gorsedd Gardens, on the lawns in front of the museum's main entrance. The museum is to the north-west of you, so face north-west with the portico in the middle of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole facade. If you're close and it won't fit, drop to 0.5x. For the dome, the sculptures and the lions, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide it a little darker if the pale stone looks washed out against the sky.
card.best_time: Pick a bright but not harsh moment so the stone shows its detail. The front faces south-east, so mornings are likely to light it best, and an early weekday should mean fewer people on the lawns.
card.selfie_here: Try the lawns of Gorsedd Gardens, between the flowerbeds and the Gorsedd stone circle, with the museum's facade right behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you have it, and hold your phone a bit low so the building fits over your shoulder. The granite steps up to the columned portico work too, with the building behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask them to stand on the paths or lawns of Gorsedd Gardens, opposite the entrance front so the whole building fits, while you pose with the museum behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: One third-party guide says selfie sticks usually need the museum's permission, so check with the museum first. It also announced a temporary closure in February 2025, so check the official site for opening times before you go.
card.challenge: Look up around the base of the dome, find the lions, and get a close-up of one that looks like it's keeping an eye on you.
card.good_to_know: The museum was founded in 1905 and got its royal charter in 1907. Building work began in 1912, but the First World War delayed it, so it opened to the public in 1922, with the official opening in 1927. The architects were Arnold Dunbar Smith and Cecil Brewer, and Sir W. Goscombe John devised the sculpture scheme.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Gorsedd Gardens, on the lawns in front of the museum's main entrance. The museum is to the north-west of you, so face north-west with the portico in the middle of your screen.

card.hook: Walk in past the fish counters and look up. There's a whole Victorian roof of ironwork up there, and you're under cover, so a rainy Cardiff day won't spoil the shot.
card.stand_here: Head into Cardiff Market through the St Mary Street or Trinity Street entrance and stand at the phone icon, right in the middle of the market. Start on the ground floor, then go up to the balcony and look down over the stalls.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the whole hall and the balcony, then 1x for stalls and signs. For the big H. Samuel clock, stand back outside the High Street entrance and try 2x or more, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the hall's upright lines straight, and tap a bright part of the screen, then slide it a little darker so the roof windows don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go during normal trading hours, when the stalls are open and busy. Check the official site for times before you set off.
card.selfie_here: Try the upper-floor balcony: switch to the front camera, use 0.5x if your phone has it, and angle yourself so the market floor and roof ironwork sit behind you. We can't promise it's a classic selfie spot, so take a couple and see what works.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask stallholders before taking close-up photos of them or their products. Works may be going on, so some areas might look different from older pictures.
card.challenge: Find the H. Samuel clock, then photograph it with a stallholder's sign or a pile of colourful fruit in the same shot.
card.good_to_know: Cardiff Market opened in May 1891 and was designed by the Borough Surveyor, William Harpur. It's been listed since 1975 and is now Grade II*. Around 60 independent traders work here, and the current clock dates from 1963, though a clock has hung there since 1910.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head into Cardiff Market through the St Mary Street or Trinity Street entrance and stand at the phone icon, right in the middle of the market. Start on the ground floor, then go up to the balcony and look down over the stalls.

card.hook: Picture a bright red footbridge, a river and a whole lot of trees, all fitting in one frame without you even trying. That's the Millennium Bridge in Bute Park, and it's an easy first photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Millennium Bridge, close to the Summerhouse kiosk by the River Taff. Face along the bridge so the red footbridge, the river and the trees fill your shot, with the park stretching away to the north.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the bridge, river and trees together. Tap 0.5x if you want to squeeze in more of the park. Try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the castle clock tower from Cooper's Field, or for details at the weir.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and sit the red bridge along one of the lower lines with trees either side, then tap the bridge and drag the slider down a touch to make it darker so the red stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the water and the red of the bridge. Autumn gives you great tree colour, but any dry day works. The light under the trees changes fast, so take a few frames of each scene.
card.selfie_here: Try the red Millennium Bridge near the Summerhouse kiosk, or Blackweir Bridge with the tumbling weir beside you. Both are bridges a Visit Wales guide lists among the park's often-photographed spots. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and tuck the bridge or weir in over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Bute Park is an open public park and free to enter, but check the official site before you go in case of closures or event set-ups.
card.challenge: Take the same bridge shot three times as the light shifts under the trees, then pick your favourite. Bonus point if your red is the reddest.
card.good_to_know: Bute Park covers 130 acres (53 ha) and was once the grounds of Cardiff Castle. It was laid out from 1873 by Andrew Pettigrew, head gardener to the 3rd Marquess of Bute, and handed to Cardiff's council in 1947. Look out for William Burges's Animal Wall, topped with sculpted animal heads.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Millennium Bridge, close to the Summerhouse kiosk by the River Taff. Face along the bridge so the red footbridge, the river and the trees fill your shot, with the park stretching away to the north.

card.hook: Castle Arcade isn't the big postcard shot of Cardiff, and that's why it's fun. You step off the street, and suddenly it's all Victorian shopfronts, signs and a narrow passage pulling your eye forward.
card.stand_here: Start on Castle Street, at the arcade's end directly opposite Cardiff Castle. Face the entrance with the castle-side street behind you, then walk in and head up to the balcony for a better view.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the entrance, since it keeps the shopfronts looking natural. Switch to zoom 0.5x inside to fit in more of the ceiling and sides, and keep your phone level so the lines don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the entrance in the middle, then tap the brightest part of the arcade and slide it a little darker so bright windows don't wash out.
card.best_time: Pick a quieter moment with the shops open, so you get fewer people in the way and a lively arcade. Check opening times before you go, because we can't confirm them. It's indoors, so the arcade's own lighting does a lot of the work.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the balcony on the upper level of Castle Arcade, which looks back over the arcade floor below. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit high, so the arcade stretches out behind you.
card.challenge: Take one vertical shot where the roof and the floor both make it in, with the shopfronts running straight down the edges of the frame.
card.good_to_know: Castle Arcade was begun in 1887 and designed by Edwin Seward for the Bute Estate. It was damaged in the Cardiff Blitz in 1941, but it was restored and still looks Victorian. In 1975 it was listed Grade II*, described as the finest of Cardiff's Victorian arcades.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start on Castle Street, at the arcade's end directly opposite Cardiff Castle. Face the entrance with the castle-side street behind you, then walk in and head up to the balcony for a better view.

selfie_spots.detail: on the upper balcony level of Castle Arcade, looking back over the arcade floor below
selfie_spots.why: Pages describe the balcony as the arcade's elevated viewpoint, so it is the one spot named for shooting the Victorian interior from above.

card.hook: Not long ago this bay was wide mud flats at low tide. Now it's a still, 500-acre freshwater lake, and Mermaid Quay sits on its edge looking very pleased with itself.
card.stand_here: Stand in Roald Dahl Plass, the open oval plaza next to the quay, and face so the Mermaid Quay buildings run along one side with the Wales Millennium Centre beyond. For a second view, the Cardiff Bay Barrage shows the quay across the water, so check the map for the exact spot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole oval, the quay buildings and the sky in one shot. Switch to 1x for a more natural look at the quay frontage, then try 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out the Wales Millennium Centre or the boats.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, use the curve of the plaza to lead the eye to the quay, tap the buildings, and drag the slider to make it a bit darker if the sky is washed out.
card.best_time: Pick a calm, bright time when the plaza isn't too crowded. Evening is also worth a go with night mode, as long as you hold your phone steady against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Try the Landsea Square water feature, the small public square with the fountain sculpture just off Mermaid Quay. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it and put the fountain behind you. I couldn't confirm the quay shows behind it, so check the view on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on New George Street facing north-east toward Mermaid Quay, while you stand ahead of them in that view.
card.rules_and_safety: Individual venues in Mermaid Quay have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for the middle of the plaza to clear, then get one shot with a wide, empty foreground and the quay lined up on the grid.
card.good_to_know: Mermaid Quay was designed by Benoy and opened in August 1999, the same year the Cardiff Bay Barrage was completed. The barrage turned the tidal bay into a freshwater lake. Roald Dahl Plass has also appeared in Doctor Who and Torchwood, so you may spot fans taking pictures too.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Roald Dahl Plass, the open oval plaza next to the quay, and face so the Mermaid Quay buildings run along one side with the Wales Millennium Centre beyond. For a second view, the Cardiff Bay Barrage shows the quay across the water, so check the map for the exact spot.

card.hook: You're standing in an old coal dock, and nothing about it looks like one. It's now a big oval stage where the dome, the pillars and a 21 m metal fountain are all there to be photographed.
card.stand_here: Stand in Roald Dahl Plass near the northern end, and face south-west toward the Wales Millennium Centre. The bronze dome should fill the background and the Pierhead Building should sit on your right.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the postcard view of the plaza, dome and Pierhead. Go to 0.5x to catch the pillars and the whole curve of the oval, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the dome or the Water Tower on its own.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the dome, then slide the brightness down a touch so the bronze and the sky don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go when the Plass is quiet so people don't fill your foreground. The pillars are lit up and look most striking after dark, so switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against your body. For the Water Tower, wait until the water is flowing, because it only runs in an on-and-off stream.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the illuminated pillars at the upper end of the Plass with the Millennium Centre behind you. Use the front camera, switch to the wider setting if your phone has one, and keep the building over your shoulder. Doctor Who and Torchwood fans also like the Torchwood pavement slab, but no source gives its exact spot, so you may need to ask someone or check a fan guide.
card.ask_someone: Stand under the footbridge at the end away from the Water Tower and look back into the bowl-shaped plaza, then ask a passer-by to take your photo from there.
card.rules_and_safety: Markets and events often fill or fence off parts of the Plass, so check the official site if you're planning around a particular view. One page calls it a safe place for children to run and cycle, away from traffic.
card.challenge: Turn round, frame the Water Tower with the pillars beside it, and take the shot just as the water is streaming down.
card.good_to_know: The oval is the old West Bute Dock, which opened in 1839 and helped make Cardiff a huge coal port. The last coal left in 1964, and the dock was later filled in. The space opened in April 2000 as the Oval Basin and was renamed after Cardiff-born author Roald Dahl in 2002.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Roald Dahl Plass near the northern end, and face south-west toward the Wales Millennium Centre. The bronze dome should fill the background and the Pierhead Building should sit on your right.

card.hook: A little white timber church sitting right on the water, with the busy colours of Mermaid Quay nearby. It's one of the easiest buildings on the Cardiff waterfront to photograph, and honestly, it does half the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Norwegian Church Arts Centre on Harbour Drive. The phone icon on the map is at the church itself, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Face the church with the open water of Cardiff Bay behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the church with the bay behind it. If you're close and the whole building won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to pick out the timber walls and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the church on one side of the frame, let the water and horizon fill the rest, and keep that horizon level.
card.best_time: There's no set time you have to come. Just check for people on the terrace before you shoot, because the church has its own café and events, and they may affect how much of the terrace you can use.
card.selfie_here: Head to the outdoor terrace outside the church, with the Cardiff Bay water behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so the church fits in with you, and check the frame before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across from the main entrance on Harbour Drive, facing west-southwest, so the whole building fits in the frame, while you stand in front of the church. It's based on a photo's position, so check it on the ground.
card.rules_and_safety: The terrace is the church's own outdoor space, and the church has a café and events. Opening arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole scene, then step in and get a close one of the timber walls and windows. Which one would you frame?
card.good_to_know: The church is a white timber building on Harbour Drive, on the edge of Cardiff Bay. The best-known picture is taken from the outdoor terrace on the bay side. Want a more traditional backdrop? Pier Head is also suggested, with the Pierhead Building behind the church, but the exact spot isn't pinned down, so check the map.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Norwegian Church Arts Centre on Harbour Drive. The phone icon on the map is at the church itself, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Face the church with the open water of Cardiff Bay behind it.

card.hook: The Pierhead Building looks like someone refused to leave any space undecorated: red terracotta, carved friezes, gargoyles, hexagonal chimneys and a clock tower, all in one go. Your phone will love it.
card.stand_here: Stand in Roald Dahl Plass, the square at the entrance to the West Bute Dock, east of the Industrial and Maritime Museum. Face across the water to the south-facing red frontage and clock tower, with the Ivor Novello statue close by.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole front and clock tower fit, then try 1x for a tidier, less stretched look. Hold your phone upright, because the building is tall and fairly close.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines to keep the tower straight, and put the Ivor Novello statue low in the foreground to add depth.
card.best_time: Summer evenings are lovely if you want the Cardiff Bay Ferris wheel lit up in your shot, and that works best from the side of the building. Otherwise, pick a day with clear light on the front.
card.selfie_here: Try Roald Dahl Plass, on the plaza between the Pierhead's front and the Senedd, with the building behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the clock tower rise over your shoulder. The Ivor Novello statue is another good backdrop, as the Pierhead can be seen from there too.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand well back on the plaza facing the bay-side (south) front and shoot upright, while you stand in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the building from the open square outside, but the inside is a visitor venue that may close for events or works, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with Ivor Novello low in the foreground and the clock tower dead straight above him. Gridlines are your friend.
card.good_to_know: The Pierhead was built in 1897 for the Bute Dock Company and designed by William Frame, who trained under William Burges. It's Grade I listed, and the clock is nicknamed "Baby Big Ben". The coat of arms on the front carries the old motto "Wrth ddŵr a thân", meaning "by water and fire".
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Roald Dahl Plass, the square at the entrance to the West Bute Dock, east of the Industrial and Maritime Museum. Face across the water to the south-facing red frontage and clock tower, with the Ivor Novello statue close by.

card.hook: A Victorian shopping arcade is hiding behind a three-storey Pennant stone and red brick front, and the little central canopy is basically asking for its photo to be taken. Grab the frame from outside first, then go in for a second one.
card.stand_here: Stand on The Hayes, opposite the arcade's Grade II entrance block at the south end of the old Morgan's department store. The arcade lies to the west of you, so face the central canopy and shopfronts.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the entrance front. If the pavement is busy and you can't step back, switch to 0.5x to fit the whole facade in. Inside, 0.5x is great for the roof and the long view of shopfronts, and 2x or more (depending on your phone) picks out the fancy details above the shops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the canopy up with the middle vertical line, then tap the brightest part of the facade and slide the brightness down a touch so the sky and stonework keep their detail.
card.best_time: Daytime gives you a clear view of the facade. An earlier, quieter hour usually means fewer people in your frame, both outside and in the passage.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the arcade's central entrance on The Hayes, under the canopy, with the entrance block behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and let the canopy and shopfronts frame you over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At the St Mary Street entrance, ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement opposite, on the Royal Hotel side, while you stand in front of the entrance block so the whole thing fits in.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside is generally fine, but ask shop staff before you spend long shooting. At busy times keep your phone handheld and move quickly so you don't block the narrow passage. Shop hours and photo rules can vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the front from The Hayes, then one looking down the passage, and see if you can spot a Venetian window or an old wooden storefront in either.
card.good_to_know: The Royal Arcade is the oldest shopping arcade in Cardiff. It was built in 1858 and is Grade II listed. It runs between The Hayes and St Mary Street, partly under the old David Morgan's department store, and was refurbished in 2007-2008. You'll still find independent shops inside, like Wally's Delicatessen and sellers of Welsh textiles, gifts and homeware.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on The Hayes, opposite the arcade's Grade II entrance block at the south end of the old Morgan's department store. The arcade lies to the west of you, so face the central canopy and shopfronts.

card.hook: Picture a fountain, flower beds and trees, with a big white stone dome and a clock tower rising behind them. That's Cardiff City Hall, and its four gilded clock dials are each 3.7 m across, so they really do glow against the sky.
card.stand_here: Stand in Alexandra Gardens, the park behind City Hall where the back of the building faces the park, and face the building. You'll get flower beds, fountain and trees in front, with the clock tower rising behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the flower beds, fountain and building into one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to home in on the clock tower and its gilded dials.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands tall instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Spring is lovely when the cherry blossom is out. Early morning is usually quieter, so fewer people wander across your picture.
card.selfie_here: Try Alexandra Gardens beside the central fountain with its statues. Use the front camera at 0.5x, turn so City Hall fills the background behind your shoulder, and look for reflections in the water. The lawn at the front, next to the rectangular pool and fountains, also works with the building rising behind you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by inside Alexandra Gardens, facing City Hall, and ask them to frame you with the clock tower and dome in view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography rules inside City Hall can vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get cherry blossom or flowers along the bottom of your shot and the clock tower standing perfectly straight at the top?
card.good_to_know: City Hall opened on 29 October 1906 and is Grade I listed. It's built of white Portland stone in the Edwardian Baroque style, and the clock tower is 59 m high. The fountains in the front pool date from 1969.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Alexandra Gardens, the park behind City Hall where the back of the building faces the park, and face the building. You'll get flower beds, fountain and trees in front, with the clock tower rising behind.

card.hook: Picture a ring of pale stone columns, and in the middle a soldier, a sailor and an airman, each holding a wreath high. It's quiet, it's tidy, and it photographs beautifully.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, on the central path of Alexandra Gardens in Cathays Park. Face the circular colonnade and let the path lead your eye straight to it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic straight-on view. Try 0.5x if you want the whole colonnade and gardens (keep the phone level), and 2x to get closer to the bronze figures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the columns up with the vertical lines, then tap the colonnade and make the picture a touch darker so the pale stone keeps its detail against the sky.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the stone and fewer people in the gardens.
card.selfie_here: Try the steps that lead down from one of the three gated porticos into the sunken circular court. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold it a little low, and let the bronze figures and the colonnade rise behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a place of remembrance, so be thoughtful and avoid intrusive shots during commemorative events.
card.challenge: Get all the columns in the frame with a little space around them, nothing cut off and the horizon dead level.
card.good_to_know: Sir Ninian Comper designed the memorial and the Prince of Wales unveiled it on 12 June 1928. It remembers those who died in the First World War, and a plaque for the Second World War was added in 1949. It is Grade II* listed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, on the central path of Alexandra Gardens in Cathays Park. Face the circular colonnade and let the path lead your eye straight to it.

selfie_spots.name: Steps down at a gated portico of the memorial colonnade, Alexandra Gardens

selfie_spots.why: Standing on the steps lowers you into the memorial's setting so the sculptural centrepiece can rise behind you, though no page names this as a selfie spot.

card.hook: A stone bear, a pack of baboons and a seal are all trying to climb over the same wall, and nobody on the pavement seems surprised. Give them a minute and you'll start picking favourites.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement to the left of the main castle entrance, facing the castle. From here the animals look like they're scrambling over the wall from the park side.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a close, straight-on shot. Try 2x to pick out one face without stepping off the pavement, or 0.5x to squeeze in the whole row. Keep your phone level so the wall doesn't bend.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line one up with the top of the wall, then tap an animal's face and slide it a little darker if the pale stone looks too bright.
card.best_time: Soft, even daylight shows off the carving best. Early in the day the pavement is likely to be quieter, so you'll get a cleaner frame.
card.selfie_here: Walk along the Castle Street pavement beside the wall, with the edge of Bute Park behind it, and stop where a few animals sit behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low so the animals peek over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on Castle Street facing the wall, where it runs along the southern edge of Bute Park, while you pose by the animals.
card.rules_and_safety: The wall is free to view from Castle Street and you don't need a ticket. Keep an eye on passing people and traffic while you line up your shot.
card.challenge: Find the anteater, the pelican and the beaver, and get all three in one photo (or a quick trio of photos if they won't line up).
card.good_to_know: William Burges designed the wall in the 1860s for the third Marquess of Bute, but it wasn't built until around 1890, after he'd died. Thomas Nicholls carved the first animals, and Alexander Carrick added six more in 1931. The wall was moved about 50 metres when the road was widened, it's Grade I listed, and the 2010 restoration gave the anteater a new nose and the animals new glass eyes.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement to the left of the main castle entrance, facing the castle. From here the animals look like they're scrambling over the wall from the park side.

sources.title: The Animal Wall • Explore The Castle • Cardiff Castle

selfie_research.notes: The pages name the best view as the southern boundary of Bute Park from Castle Street, but none of them names a precise selfie position with the wall directly behind the visitor, so both spots are approximate. The ask-someone spot is the best overall view, not a page-named photographer position; treat it as a general vantage. Sources disagree on the relocation date (1923, 1928, or 1931) and on the postcode (CF10 1BJ vs CF10 1BT); these do not affect the spots. No page gives selfie stick or tripod rules, and no page gives a safety point. The supplied coordinates are close to the wall's Castle Street stretch but were not checked against a map.

card.hook: Picture a 500-year-old tower rising over a street of ordinary shops, like it wandered in and decided to stay. That's Church Street in Cardiff, and the tower at the end of it is the star.
card.stand_here: Stand on Church Street and look down the street toward the church tower, which closes off the far end. That's the straight-on postcard view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the street and the tower in together. If the tower won't fit, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the battlements and pinnacles, using the zoom buttons rather than pinching.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright so the grey stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early in the day the street is likely to be quieter, which gives you a cleaner view. Soft daylight suits the grey stone best.
card.selfie_here: Try the little churchyard garden behind the church: stand among the old gravestones with the tower behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x and hold the phone a bit low so the tower fits over your shoulder. You can also walk up to the foot of the tower near its entrance on St John Street, where it rises right behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take the photo from Church Street while you stand further down the street toward the church, so the whole tower fits at the end of the street behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The church interior and churchyard garden may have set opening times, so check the official site before you go. If you want to climb the tower, check that too, as access may be limited.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with a few people in the street to show how tall the tower is, then one close-up of the battlements. Which one looks more like a postcard?
card.good_to_know: The church dates back to 1180 and was rebuilt in the later 1400s after being sacked in 1404. The pinnacled tower is usually dated to about 1490 and is over 40 metres high. Apart from Cardiff Castle, it's the only medieval building left in the city centre.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Church Street and look down the street toward the church tower, which closes off the far end. That's the straight-on postcard view.

selfie_research.notes: Sources name no selfie-stick or tripod rules, and no safety point. The churchyard garden spot is inferred from sources that describe the garden behind the church, not from a page that calls it a selfie spot; the visitor-facing 'with the tower behind' framing is my reading. The tower is climbable only on the last Saturday of each month according to one guide, and another says summer only, so check before visiting. Only two selfie spots were found, and sources are thin on exact positions, so verify on a map.
